messages.subject: Modeling Observer Bias
messages.body_plain:
Greetings Distance-Users-

I'd like to find out if any of you have experience modeling the effects of =
increasing observer bias in distance estimation upon density estimates.  =
We have a number of years of data (9) with a large number of bird species =
(210) collected from 32 point transects (10 point each) using a number of =
observers (19).  We have enough data to conduct density analyses for about =
40 bird species, and these analyses strongly imply increased bias in =
distance estimations from the last 4 years of the study.  Six observers =
were present in 3 or more years, and the growth in apparent bias is =
strongest in these six ( to judge from simple distribution plots of =
detection distances by observer by year)

My initial question goes to how best to model this observer bias when most =
observers did not have enough detections to attempt a species-by year-by =
observer stratification (e.g., 398-399 in example 8.7 in the Distance =
Sampling book, though a few do and I'm working on these at present).

My second question goes to can/should one use all detections from all =
species for an observer in a given year to estimate observer bias in =
distance estimations for a single bird species?

Any help you can given or light you can shed would be much appreciated.

Cheers -Russ

Russell Norvell, Avian Ecologist
Non-game Avian Program, UDWR

Distance 4.0 Beta 1 is now available for download via the world-wide web.

The web site address for download is:

Distance 4.0 is a major update over the previous version (3.5).  New features
include automated survey design and a new analysis engine that allows
multiple-covariates in the detection function. More information about the new
features is on the web site.  There are also details of the new email
discussion group, distace-sampling-D4Beta.  We encourage all users of
Distance 4.0 to join this group.

The current release is a public beta, released to give you a chance to try
out the new functionality.  It is intended for use by more advanced users --
if you are new to distance sampling we recommend you use Distance 3.5 for
now.

One exception to the above is people who use Spanish language versions of
Windows.  A bug in Microsoft Visual Basic prevented them from accessing
Distance 3.5 -- this has now been circumvented in Distance 4.0.

We hope you enjoy using the new software, and apologise for it being released
rather later than expected.  We expect to release the full version before the
ICODS conference this summer.

messages.subject: Answer: A question about binning
messages.body_plain:
Hi Steve,

I'm posting my reply to the distance-sampling list, as your question raises
several points of general interest.  My answer is given below your message.

On Wed, 14 Mar 2001 10:33:19 +1300, Steve Dawson wrote:

> >Dear Len,
> >
> >I hope you don't mind if I ask you a question directly. I would very much
> >appreciate your advice.
> >
> >With our latest data set (an aerial survey of dolphins) we've experimented
> >with binnings to achieve the smoothest possible histogram, which, by
> >intuition, should be the easiest to model. Having found "good" cutpoints,
> >there seem to be two ways to use them in Distance (3.5):
> >
> >(1). In the "data filter", enter those as manual cutpoints in the
> >"intervals" screen and group the data for analysis. This truncates the data
> >past the last cutpoint. While doing this does throw some information away
> >(the exact distance of each sighting), it does force the fitting process to
> >use the "best" cutpoints.
> >
> >In our case doing this results in an ESW of 250.86m (CV=5.32%).
> >
> >(2). If we do not specify cutpoints in the "data filter", but choose a
> >truncation level, then go to the "model" screen, choose "diagnostics" and
> >"detection function" we can enter cutpoints to use for the GOF testing.
> >
> >Doing this results in an ESW of 240.50m (CV=5.98%).
> >
> >In "Distance" I have found little explicit advice on what to do. It says
> >you can analyse data as grouped if they are problematic (i.e. show heaping
> >or rounding), implying that if they are not problematic you should not
> >group the data for analysis. Our data are not problematic, but with
> >appropriate binning we can smooth the histogram considerably.
> >
> >It seems to me that what is happening at (1) is that we are forcing
> >Distance to use those cutpoints to fit the detection function. If we choose
> >(2), Distance chooses a set of arbitary cutpoints, and uses those to
> >estimate the detection function, but then uses our cutpoints to evaluate
> >GOF. It seems to my meagre brain that if by experimentation we have found
> >really good cutpoints, we SHOULD use them, and take the approach in (1).
> >
> >What do you think?
> >
> >Cheers,
> >
> >________________
> >Dr Steve Dawson, Senior Lecturer
> >Trustee, New Zealand Whale and Dolphin Trust
> >Marine Science Department, Otago University
> >P.O. Box 56, Dunedin, New Zealand.

Specifying interval cutpoints in the Data Filter has a different effect from
specifying them in the Model Definition (under Detection Function |
Diagnostics), and is used for a different reason.

You choose intervals in the Data Filter if you want the data to be *analyzed*
as interval (grouped/binned) data.  You would do this if (i) your data were
actually collected in intervals, or (ii) you are trying to work around some
problem in the data, such as evasive movement.

If neither of these are the case, you are almost always better to leave your
data as exact, and not put it into intervals for the analysis.  By putting
your distances into intervals, you are throwing information away and may
therefore get a less reliable result.  In many cases, you will get worse
precision using intervals - but not in all cases.  It is quite possible to
fiddle around with the cutpoints until you get a lower CV than in the exact
data -- but are the results more reliable?  Doing an analysis 20 different
ways and choosing the answer with the lowest CV is rarely the best policy.
So, I believe its usually best to convert exact data into intervals only if
you're trying to fix a specific problem.  Perhaps others have a different
perspective on this?

You choose interval cutpoints in the Model Definition (under Detection
Function | Diagnostics) when your data is collected and analyzed as exact,
and you want to fine-tune the goodness of fit histograms and tests that
Distance produces.  Note that in this case, the data are *not changed* - they
are analyzed as exact.  Only the histograms and the goodness of fit
statistics are changed.  (You can easily confirm this for yourself in
Distance -- try changing the cutpoints in Diagnostics and confirm that the
estimated ESW doesn't change at all.)

Note that if you define intervals in the Data Filter, then your data are
already put into intervals by the time they arrive at the Model Definition.
In this case, any intervals you specify in the Diagnostics page are ignored
-- the intervals you get for histograms and goodness of fit are those you
specified in the Data Filter.

Why would you want to fiddle with the cutpoints for histograms and goodness-
of-fit for your exact data?  Firstly, you would do this to look for potential
problems in your data during exploratory data analysis.  For example, you can
look for a spike at (or close) to 0 distance, by defining lots of small
intervals at small distances (e.g., for a study with a truncation distance of
100 meters and lots of observations you could have cutpoints of 0, 1, 2, 3,
4, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100).  You can look for
rounding by defining cutpoints that bracket the rounding peaks (e.g., if you
suspect rounding to the nearest 10 meters, define cutpoints of 0, 1, 9, 11,
19, 21, 29, 31, etc).  You get the idea: you're looking for potential
problems with the distance data, and defining the cutpoints so as to best
help you identify and diagnose them.

The second reason for changing cutpoints in Diagnostics is to make a nicer
detection function for putting in your publication.  I would almost always
recommend putting a figure showing the data and fitted detection function in
any publication that uses distance sampling.  In this case, you don't want
nearly as many cutpoints as in the exploratory phase, but you may not want
the equal cutpoints that Distance gives by default either.  For example, you
could have larger cutpoint intervals further from the line, where there are
less data and the fit is not so critical (one rule of thumb is to choose
cutpoints such that the number of observations in each interval is similar).
I don't have a strong opinion about how histograms should look in
publications -- perhaps others do?

Of course, how you define intervals for your histogram will also affect the
chi-sq goodness-of-fit statistic you get out.  This is great in the
exploratory phase, but seems a bit of a shame in the confirmation/publication
phase -- when refereeing a publication you may suspect that the authors have
manipulated their intervals to get the best possible goodness-of-fit, and
hide any problems! On a less paranoid level, it is rather arbitrary.  In a
future version of Distance, we hope to add Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramer-von
Mises goodness-of-fit statistics to the list -- both of these can be applied
to continuous as well as discrete data, so for exact distances they won't be
affected by the histogram bins.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator
Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland KY16 9SS

messages.subject: CONFERENCE: ICODS, 2nd announcement
messages.body_plain:
-------------------------------------------------
               INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON DISTANCE SAMPLING
                    Estimating wildlife abundance for
                   Ecology, Management and Conservation

                         July 30 - August 3, 2001
                          St. Andrews, Scotland

                     http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/icods/
             -------------------------------------------------
                             SECOND ANNOUNCEMENT
             -------------------------------------------------

PLEASE NOTE:
THE DEADLINE FOR ABSTRACTS IS **MARCH 30th**.  IF YOU ARE PLANNING ON GIVING
A TALK OR POSTER PLEASE CONTACT THE CONFERENCE ORGANIZER BEFORE THAT DATE.

Invitation
----------

We invite you to participate in the first International Conference on
Distance Sampling, to be held on July 30 - August 3, 2001 in St. Andrews,
Scotland.  This announcement contains outline information about the
conference and linked workshops.  Please visit our web site for more
details.

Objectives
----------

The aim of this conference is to bring together for the first time all those
interested in the estimation of wildlife abundance using distance sampling
methods. Determining the density or abundance of wildlife populations is a
key component of population ecology, wildlife management and biological
conservation. For many taxa, distance sampling methods such as line
transects, point transects (variable circular plots) and trapping webs are
the most efficient approach.  These methods are now in very widespread use by
biologists, and there have been many recent developments in the underlying
theory that increase the scope of the methods.  The time is right for a major
international gathering.

Our major objectives are to:

-Bring together practitioners from a wide range of disciplines and systems,
as well as statisticians involved in methodological development

-Present examples of new research and best practice through invited plenary
talks

-Provide a forum for the exchange of ideas, techniques and methods through
contributed talks, posters and informal discussion sessions

-Provide world-class training for those new to the subject, through linked
workshops to be held before and after the conference

We hope that the conference will prove to be a major milestone in the
application of wildlife survey techniques, leading to increased effectiveness
of field studies and stimulating many new areas of research.

Conference program
------------------

The conference will be a mix of plenary papers, giving state of the art
reviews of theory and practice, and contributed papers and posters.  In
addition, meeting rooms will be available for delegates to schedule and
attend informal discussion groups on topics of their choice.

The following leading experts in the field have agreed to give plenary
papers. (The preliminary topic of their paper is given in brackets.)

- Colin Bibby
  Birdlife International, Cambridge, UK
  (Estimation of bird abundance and its relevance to conservation.)

- David L. Borchers
  University of St Andrews, UK
  (Unified models for estimating wildlife abundance.)

- Stephen T. Buckland
  University of St Andrews, UK
  (Overview of research linked to the Distance4 project.)

- Kenneth P.  Burnham
  Colorado Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit, Colorado, USA
  (Large scale, long term monitoring.)

- Jeffrey L. Laake
  National Marine Mammal Lab, Seattle, USA
  (Distance sampling of Antarctic pack ice seals.)

- Bryan F.J. Manly
  University of Otago, Dunedin, New Zealand
  (Simultaneous estimation of population size and habitat selection by
  distance sampling.)

- Kenneth H. Pollock
  North Carolina State University, USA
  (Combining capture recapture and distance sampling, or Comparisons of
  detectability estimation methods for circular plots on birds.)

- Fred L. Ramsey
  Oregon State University, USA
  (A general paradigm for all variable area survey procedures.)

We encourage delegates to consider contributing oral or poster papers. We
welcome contributions on any aspect of distance sampling, from practical,
taxon-specific issues to new methodological developments.  The deadline for
abstracts is 30th March 2001.  More details are given on the conference web
site under Call for Papers.

In addition to the scientific program, we are planning field trips and a full
social program.

Linked Workshops
----------------

The conference will be bracketed by two linked workshops. The aim of these
workshops is to train participants in the latest methods for design and
analysis of distance sampling surveys, including line and point transects.
The workshops are taught by leading researchers in the field, using
industry-standard software.

- Workshop 1: Introduction to Distance Sampling, July 25-27
An introductory workshop, focusing on "conventional" distance sampling
methods, including line and point transects where detection on the trackline
or point is certain.  The workshop will be a blend of theory and practice and
participants will learn how to use the program Distance.  Participants will
gain a solid grounding in both survey design and methods of analysis for
distance sampling surveys.

- Workshop 2: Advanced Techniques and Recent Developments in Distance
  Sampling, August 6-8
A workshop designed for those who are already familiar with the basics, where
we will teach advanced material such as automated survey design, adaptive
sampling, incorporating covariates into the detection function, methods for
where g0<1, and spatial modeling of density.  Participants will learn some of
the more advanced features of Distance.  This workshop will take place after
the conference to give us a chance to discuss new work presented there.

For both workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data sets,
and can expect to do some preliminary analyses with their data.

The number of participants on both workshops is strictly limited and, based
on preliminary registrations, we expect both workshops to be oversubscribed.
To avoid disappointment, we encourage you to register for these as soon as
possible.

Sponsors
--------

ICODS is supported by the UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research
Council and the Biometrics Working Group of the Wildlife Society.

Further information
-------------------

More information about the conference, including the registration form,
is at the conference web site: http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/icods/

If you would like a printed copy of this information or have any
questions about the conference, please contact:

I'm reviewing a paper where the authors simply calculated the effective
strip width and then multiplied the number of ALL BIRDS (out to all
distances including those beyond the ESW) by the area surveyed within the
ESW by transect length.  It seems to me that this would report the same
density or overall population size as DISTANCE but bot report any error
values.

Any thoughts?

thanks,

messages.subject: Re: effective strip width
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben (and distance list),

Yes, you're right, assuming they didn't truncate some of the data at the
analysis stage to estimate their ESW.

If they did truncate, then density is number of birds seen **within the
truncation boundary** divided by the effective search area.  (Effective search
area is 2 x total transect length x ESW.)

 - Len
